content: 1. What is the ideal dietary composition for patients undergoing treatment for active tuberculosis (TB)? Do newly diagnosed TB patients have increased energy requirements? The population of interest includes infants, children, adolescents, adults, and pregnant or lactating women. The intervention focuses on individuals with TB, while the control group consists of healthy individuals. Critical outcomes include resting energy expenditure and total energy expenditure, applicable across all settings, including emergency situations. 2. Should macronutrient supplementation be recommended to enhance TB treatment and health outcomes in well-nourished or undernourished patients receiving treatment for active TB? Does macronutrient supplementation, provided as food or high-energy supplements, improve TB treatment outcomes? Does macronutrient supplementation, provided as food or high-energy supplements, enhance nutritional recovery and quality of life? The population includes infants, children, adolescents, adults, and pregnant or lactating women. Subpopulations are categorized by nutritional status (underweight or not), HIV status (positive or negative), antiretroviral therapy (ART) use (on ART or not), TB resistance (MDR-TB or XDR-TB), vulnerability (e.g., homelessness, alcohol use, intravenous drug use), income classification (low-, middle-, or high-income countries), food security (secure or insecure), and displacement/refugee status. Interventions include on-site or off-site daily, weekly, or monthly rations, as well as nutrient-dense supplements. Controls involve standard care, with or without dietary advice, or head-to-head trials. Critical outcomes include TB treatment success (e.g., cure, treatment completion), nutritional recovery (e.g. These considerations apply to all settings, including emergencies. 3. Should micronutrient supplementation be included as part of routine care for well-nourished or undernourished patients being treated for active TB to improve treatment and nutritional outcomes? Does routine daily multi-micronutrient supplementation improve TB treatment outcomes? Does routine daily multi-micronutrient supplementation enhance nutritional recovery and quality of life? The population includes infants, children, adolescents, adults, and pregnant or lactating women. Subpopulations are defined by nutritional status (underweight or not), HIV status (positive or negative), ART use (on ART or not), TB resistance (MDR-TB or XDR-TB), vulnerability (e.g., homelessness, alcohol use, intravenous drug use), income classification (low-, middle-, or high-income countries), food security (secure or insecure), and displacement/refugee status. Interventions include single micronutrient supplements (e.g., vitamin A, C, D, E, zinc, iron, selenium) or multi-micronutrient supplements. Are there population-level nutritional interventions that could reduce the progression from latent to active TB among household contacts of patients with active TB? This question explores whether nutritional strategies at the population level can prevent the development of active TB in individuals exposed to TB within their households.
